question: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
title: HTTP vs HTTPS – Java Backend Security Basics
direct_answer: **HTTP** sends data in **plaintext** over the network, so anyone in between can read or tamper with it. **HTTPS** is HTTP layered over **TLS**, which adds **encryption** (no eavesdropping), **integrity** (no tampering), and **authentication** (you're really talking to the right server, via its certificate). HTTPS uses port **443** vs HTTP's **80**, and is mandatory for anything carrying credentials, tokens, or personal data — browsers now mark plain HTTP as "Not Secure".

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know HTTPS = HTTP + TLS and the three guarantees it adds (confidentiality, integrity, authentication)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying HTTPS 'just encrypts' and forgetting integrity and server authentication; thinking it protects data at rest
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name all three guarantees and note HTTPS protects data in transit only, not in your database

sections.title: HTTP vs HTTPS: Adding the TLS Layer
sections.content:
**HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) sends requests and responses as **plaintext**. Anyone on the network path — a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot, an ISP, an attacker doing a man-in-the-middle — can **read** the data and even **modify** it in flight. That's fine for a static public page, but catastrophic for passwords, tokens, or personal data.

**HTTPS** is simply **HTTP running over TLS** (Transport Layer Security). TLS wraps the connection and adds **three guarantees**: **confidentiality** (data is encrypted, so eavesdroppers see gibberish), **integrity** (tampering is detected), and **authentication** (the server proves its identity with a **certificate** signed by a trusted Certificate Authority, so you know you're talking to the real `bank.com`).

HTTP uses port **80**, HTTPS uses port **443**. A key limitation to state: HTTPS protects data **in transit only** — it does nothing for data **at rest** in your database, which still needs hashing/encryption. Modern browsers mark plain HTTP as **"Not Secure"**, so HTTPS is effectively mandatory.

sections.title: What TLS Adds to HTTP
sections.content:
emerald|Confidentiality|~Encryption|eavesdroppers see gibberish|protects credentials/tokens|symmetric session key
blue|Integrity|~Tamper detection|data can't be altered silently|MAC on each record|detects modification
violet|Authentication|~Server identity|certificate from a CA|you reach the real server|stops impersonation
amber|Scope|~In transit only|not data at rest|DB still needs hashing|port 443 vs 80

sections.title: HTTP vs HTTPS
sections.content:
| Aspect | HTTP | HTTPS |
|---|---|---|
| Data on the wire | Plaintext | Encrypted (TLS) |
| Eavesdropping | Readable by anyone | Protected |
| Tampering | Undetected | Detected (integrity) |
| Server identity | Unverified | Verified via certificate |
| Port | 80 | 443 |
| Browser label | "Not Secure" | Padlock |

sections.title: Enabling HTTPS in Spring Boot
sections.content:
```properties
# application.properties — terminate TLS in the app (often a proxy does this instead)
server.port=8443
server.ssl.enabled=true
server.ssl.key-store=classpath:keystore.p12
server.ssl.key-store-type=PKCS12
server.ssl.key-store-password=${SSL_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD}
```
```java
// Redirect any plain HTTP request to HTTPS at the Spring Security layer
http.requiresChannel(c -> c.anyRequest().requiresSecure());
```
*In production, TLS is often terminated at a load balancer/reverse proxy; the app then trusts forwarded headers.*

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HTTPS = HTTP + TLS**; HTTP is plaintext, HTTPS is encrypted.
- TLS provides **confidentiality, integrity, and authentication** — not just encryption.
- The server proves identity with a **CA-signed certificate**.
- HTTP uses port **80**, HTTPS uses port **443**.
- HTTPS protects data **in transit only** — data at rest still needs its own protection.
- Browsers flag plain HTTP as **"Not Secure"**, so HTTPS is mandatory for real apps.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HTTP sends everything in plaintext over the network, which means anyone sitting in between — a rogue Wi-Fi access point, an ISP, or an attacker doing a man-in-the-middle — can read the data and even modify it in transit. That's a disaster for anything sensitive like passwords or tokens. HTTPS fixes this, and the simplest way to describe it is that HTTPS is just HTTP running over TLS, which is Transport Layer Security.

What TLS adds is really three guarantees, and I'd name all three because a lot of people only mention encryption. The first is confidentiality — the data is encrypted, so an eavesdropper just sees gibberish. The second is integrity — if someone tampers with the data in flight, it's detected, so the message can't be silently altered. And the third, which people often forget, is authentication: the server proves its identity using a certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority. That's how your browser knows it's actually talking to the real bank dot com and not an impostor.

A couple of concrete details: HTTP runs on port 80 and HTTPS on port 443. And an important limitation to state is that HTTPS only protects data in transit — it does nothing for data sitting in your database, so passwords still need to be hashed and sensitive data still needs encryption at rest. These days browsers actively label plain HTTP sites as Not Secure, so HTTPS is effectively mandatory for any real application. In a Spring Boot app you can enable TLS with the server dot ssl properties, though in production it's often terminated at a load balancer in front of the app.

beats.label: what tls adds
beats.content: TLS gives you three guarantees that HTTP lacks. Confidentiality: data is encrypted in transit, unreadable to anyone intercepting the connection. Integrity: any tampering with the data in transit is detectable. Authenticity: a certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority proves you're talking to the real server, not an impersonator sitting in the middle.

beats.label: practical impact
beats.content: Without HTTPS, a user on the same Wi-Fi network as your API can intercept JWTs, session cookies, and passwords in plaintext. That's why no production API should ever run on HTTP. In Spring Boot, the usual pattern is TLS termination at an Nginx reverse proxy or load balancer, with the app running on plain HTTP internally.

beats.label: sharp edge
beats.content: sharp edge: saying 'HTTPS encrypts everything' without naming the three guarantees sounds vague. Interviewers at security-conscious companies will follow up. Know confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity by name.

question: How does TLS handshake work at a high level?
title: TLS Handshake Explained – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: The **TLS handshake** is how client and server agree on encryption before any data flows. At a high level: the client sends **ClientHello** (supported versions/ciphers + random), the server replies **ServerHello** plus its **certificate**; the client **verifies the certificate** against trusted CAs, they perform a **key exchange** (e.g. ECDHE) to derive a shared **symmetric session key**, and both send **Finished** messages. After that, all application data is encrypted with the fast **symmetric** key. The handshake uses slow **asymmetric** crypto only to safely establish that symmetric key.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the handshake authenticates the server and bootstraps a symmetric session key via asymmetric crypto
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the whole session uses asymmetric encryption; not mentioning certificate verification
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the asymmetric-to-symmetric handoff (why) and that TLS 1.3 streamlined the handshake to one round trip

sections.title: Negotiating a Secure Channel
sections.content:
Before HTTPS can send a single byte of real data, the client and server run the **TLS handshake** — a short negotiation that establishes **who the server is** and **what key to encrypt with**.

The clever part is the mix of two kinds of cryptography. **Asymmetric** crypto (public/private keys, certificates) is **secure but slow**; **symmetric** crypto (one shared key) is **fast but needs both sides to share a secret**. The handshake uses asymmetric crypto **only briefly** — to authenticate the server and safely agree on a shared **symmetric session key** — and then switches to that fast symmetric key for the actual data. That handoff is the whole point of the handshake.

It also **authenticates** the server: the server presents a **certificate**, and the client checks it's signed by a trusted **CA**, not expired, and matches the hostname. **TLS 1.3** streamlined all this into roughly **one round trip**.

sections.title: TLS Handshake (high level)
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: ClientHello (versions, ciphers, random)
    S->>C: ServerHello (chosen cipher, random)
    S->>C: Certificate (public key, signed by CA)
    C->>C: Verify certificate vs trusted CAs
    C->>S: Key exchange (e.g. ECDHE)
    Note over C,S: Both derive the same symmetric session key
    C->>S: Finished (encrypted)
    S->>C: Finished (encrypted)
    Note over C,S: Application data now encrypted with symmetric key
```

sections.title: Observing the Handshake
Step by Step
sections.content:
1. **ClientHello** — the client lists supported TLS versions and cipher suites and sends a random value.
2. **ServerHello + Certificate** — the server picks a cipher, sends its own random, and presents its **certificate** (containing its public key).
3. **Certificate verification** — the client confirms the cert is **signed by a trusted CA**, **not expired**, and **matches the hostname**. This is the authentication step.
4. **Key exchange** — using a key-agreement algorithm (modern TLS uses **ECDHE** for forward secrecy), both sides independently derive the **same symmetric session key** without ever sending it.
5. **Finished** — both send an encrypted `Finished` message to confirm the handshake wasn't tampered with. From here, **all data uses the symmetric key**.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- The handshake **authenticates the server** and **establishes a symmetric session key** before data flows.
- It uses **asymmetric crypto briefly** (slow but secure) to agree on a **symmetric key** (fast) for the session.
- Certificate verification checks **CA signature, expiry, and hostname**.
- Modern key exchange (**ECDHE**) gives **forward secrecy**.
- **TLS 1.3** reduced the handshake to about **one round trip**.
- After the handshake, **all application data is symmetrically encrypted**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The TLS handshake is the negotiation that happens before HTTPS sends any real data, and its job is two things: prove who the server is, and agree on a key to encrypt with. The clever idea at the center of it is mixing two kinds of cryptography. Asymmetric cryptography, which uses public and private keys and certificates, is very secure but slow. Symmetric cryptography uses a single shared key and is fast, but both sides have to share that secret. So the handshake uses the slow asymmetric crypto only briefly — just long enough to authenticate the server and safely agree on a shared symmetric key — and then it switches to that fast symmetric key for the actual data. That handoff is really the whole point.

Step by step, it starts with the client sending a ClientHello, which lists the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports along with a random value. The server responds with a ServerHello, picking the cipher, and sends its certificate, which contains its public key. The client then verifies that certificate — it checks that it's signed by a trusted Certificate Authority, that it hasn't expired, and that it matches the hostname it's connecting to. That's the authentication step. Then the two sides do a key exchange — modern TLS uses something called ECDHE — and from that, both independently derive the same symmetric session key without ever actually transmitting it. Finally, each side sends an encrypted Finished message to confirm nothing was tampered with, and from that point on all the application data is encrypted with the symmetric key. One nice detail to add is that TLS 1.3 streamlined this down to roughly a single round trip, so it's much faster than older versions.

beats.label: the handshake in plain english
beats.content: The client says hello and lists the encryption algorithms it supports. The server picks one and sends its certificate. The certificate contains the server's public key and is signed by a Certificate Authority the client trusts. The client verifies the signature to confirm it's talking to the real server, not an impersonator.

beats.label: key exchange
beats.content: Next they agree on a shared secret. The client generates a session key, encrypts it with the server's public key, and sends it over. Only the server has the matching private key to decrypt it. Now both sides have the same session key and switch to fast symmetric encryption (AES) for all actual data.

beats.label: candidates miss
beats.content: candidates miss: saying 'HTTPS uses RSA to encrypt all the data.' No — asymmetric encryption is only used for the key exchange step because it's slow. All actual data is encrypted with AES, which is orders of magnitude faster. That's the hybrid model.

question: What is a TLS certificate and what information does it contain?
title: TLS Certificates Explained – Java Backend Developer Guide
direct_answer: A **TLS certificate** is a digital document that **binds a public key to an identity** (a domain name) and is **signed by a Certificate Authority (CA)** that browsers trust. It contains the **subject** (domain), the **public key**, the **issuer** (CA), a **validity period** (not-before/not-after), the **serial number**, **Subject Alternative Names (SANs)**, and the CA's **digital signature**. During the handshake the client uses it to **verify the server's identity** — checking the CA signature, expiry, and that the hostname matches a SAN.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know a certificate binds a public key to a domain and is trusted via a CA's signature
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the certificate contains the private key, or that it 'is' the encryption; ignoring expiry and hostname/SAN checks
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention SANs (modern hostname matching), the chain of trust to a root CA, and that the private key stays on the server

sections.title: A Signed Binding of Key to Identity
sections.content:
A **TLS certificate** (often called an SSL certificate) is a digital document that **binds a public key to an identity** — typically a domain name — and is **signed by a Certificate Authority (CA)**. The signature is what makes it trustworthy: browsers and operating systems ship with a list of trusted root CAs, so a certificate signed by one (directly or through intermediates) is automatically trusted.

Crucially, the certificate contains the **public** key, never the **private** key. The private key stays secret on the server and is what proves the server actually owns the certificate. Anyone can read a certificate; only the legitimate server can complete the handshake with the matching private key.

During the handshake the client uses the certificate to **authenticate the server**: it verifies the **CA signature** (chain of trust up to a trusted root), that it's **within its validity period**, and that the requested **hostname matches** one of the certificate's **Subject Alternative Names (SANs)**.

sections.title: What's Inside a TLS Certificate
sections.content:
blue|Subject|~The identity|domain / hostname|matched via SANs|who the cert is for
emerald|Public key|~For key exchange|paired with server's private key|private key stays on server|never inside the cert
violet|Issuer + signature|~Chain of trust|signed by a CA|root CA in browser store|makes it trustworthy
amber|Validity + serial|~Lifecycle|not-before / not-after|expiry must be valid|serial for revocation

sections.title: Inspecting a Certificate
sections.content:
```bash
# View the fields of a live certificate
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
```
```text
subject= CN=example.com
issuer=  C=US, O=DigiCert Inc, CN=DigiCert TLS RSA SHA256 2020 CA1
notBefore=Jan  1 00:00:00 2026 GMT
notAfter =Apr  1 23:59:59 2026 GMT
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:example.com, DNS:www.example.com
```
*The client checks subject/SAN against the hostname, the issuer chain to a trusted root, and the dates.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking the cert holds the private key**: it holds the **public** key; the private key stays on the server.
- **Ignoring SANs**: modern browsers match the hostname against **SANs**, not the legacy Common Name.
- **Forgetting expiry**: an **expired** certificate fails verification — automate renewal (e.g. Let's Encrypt).
- **Self-signed in production**: not trusted by browsers; use a CA-issued certificate.
- **Missing intermediates**: serve the **full chain** or some clients can't build the path to the root.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A TLS certificate **binds a public key to a domain** and is **signed by a CA**.
- It contains: **subject, public key, issuer, validity dates, serial, SANs, CA signature**.
- The **private key is never in the certificate** — it stays on the server.
- Verification checks **CA chain of trust, validity period, and hostname/SAN match**.
- Browsers match the hostname against **SANs**, not the old Common Name.
- Use **CA-issued** certs (not self-signed) in production and serve the **full chain**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A TLS certificate, which people often call an SSL certificate, is a digital document that binds a public key to an identity — usually a domain name — and it's signed by a Certificate Authority. That signature is what makes it trustworthy: browsers and operating systems ship with a built-in list of trusted root CAs, so if a certificate is signed by one of them, directly or through intermediate authorities, it's automatically trusted.

In terms of what it actually contains: there's the subject, which is the identity the certificate is for, like the domain name; the public key; the issuer, which is the CA that signed it; a validity period with a not-before and a not-after date; a serial number; the Subject Alternative Names, or SANs, which list the hostnames the certificate is valid for; and the CA's digital signature. One really important point to get right is that the certificate contains only the public key, never the private key. The private key stays secret on the server, and it's what proves the server genuinely owns that certificate — anyone can read a certificate, but only the real server can complete the handshake with the matching private key.

During the handshake, the client uses the certificate to authenticate the server. It verifies three things: that the certificate is signed by a trusted CA, following the chain of trust up to a trusted root; that it's currently within its validity period and hasn't expired; and that the hostname it's connecting to matches one of the SANs. A couple of things that make you stand out are knowing that modern browsers match against SANs rather than the old Common Name field, and that in production you always use a CA-issued certificate and serve the full chain including intermediates, so clients can build the path to the root.

An X.509 certificate holds:
- The domain(s) it's valid for
- The server's public key
- Validity dates (not before, not after)

beats.label: cert vs private key
beats.content: The certificate is public. Every client that connects receives a copy during the handshake. The private key is secret and never transmitted. That's the critical distinction. If your private key leaks, anyone can impersonate your server. If your certificate leaks, nothing happens.

beats.label: non-obvious
beats.content: non-obvious: Let's Encrypt provides free 90-day certificates with Certbot handling auto-renewal. There's no excuse for self-signed certs in production. Self-signed is fine for local dev because no chain of trust is needed when you control both ends.

question: What is HSTS and why should your API use it?
title: HSTS – HTTP Strict Transport Security for Java APIs
direct_answer: **HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)** is a response header (`Strict-Transport-Security`) that tells the browser to **only ever talk to your domain over HTTPS** for a given duration (`max-age`), automatically upgrading any `http://` attempt and refusing to connect if the certificate is invalid. It defeats **SSL-stripping** man-in-the-middle attacks and protects that risky first redirect from HTTP to HTTPS. Use it with a long `max-age`, `includeSubDomains`, and ideally `preload` once you're confident HTTPS works everywhere.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know HSTS forces HTTPS at the browser and prevents SSL-stripping downgrade attacks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing HSTS with the TLS cert itself; enabling preload prematurely; not understanding the first-visit gap
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain SSL stripping and how HSTS closes the redirect window, plus the caution that a wrong max-age/preload can lock users out

sections.title: Forcing HTTPS at the Browser
sections.content:
**HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)** is a response header that instructs the browser: **for the next `max-age` seconds, only connect to this domain over HTTPS**. After the browser sees it once, it will **automatically upgrade** any `http://` link to `https://` *before* sending the request, and it will **refuse to connect at all** if the certificate is invalid (no click-through).

The attack it stops is **SSL stripping**. Normally a site redirects `http://` to `https://`, but that **first plaintext request** can be intercepted by a man-in-the-middle who keeps the connection on HTTP and proxies HTTPS to the server — the user never notices. HSTS closes that window: once the policy is cached, the browser never makes the plaintext request in the first place.

You enable it with a long **`max-age`** (e.g. one year), **`includeSubDomains`** to cover everything, and optionally **`preload`** to be hardcoded into browsers' built-in lists (so even the very first visit is protected). The caution: with `preload`/long `max-age`, if HTTPS later breaks you **can't fall back** — only enable it when HTTPS is solid everywhere.

sections.title: HSTS Directives and Effect
sections.content:
emerald|max-age|~How long to enforce|seconds, e.g. 31536000|browser remembers HTTPS-only|core directive
blue|includeSubDomains|~Coverage|applies to all subdomains|protects api., www.|enable when all use HTTPS
violet|preload|~First-visit safety|hardcoded in browsers|removes the initial gap|only when confident
amber|Stops|~SSL stripping|no plaintext first request|downgrade attack blocked|no cert click-through

sections.title: Enabling HSTS in Spring Security
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing HSTS with the certificate**: HSTS is a *policy header*; the certificate is the *identity proof*. Different things.
- **Enabling `preload` too early**: getting onto the preload list is hard to undo — only do it when HTTPS works everywhere.
- **Huge `max-age` before you're ready**: if HTTPS breaks, users are locked out for that whole duration.
- **Sending HSTS over HTTP**: browsers ignore it on plaintext; it only takes effect over HTTPS.
- **Forgetting subdomains**: without `includeSubDomains`, an `http://api.` request can still be stripped.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HSTS forces the browser to use HTTPS only** for your domain for `max-age` seconds.
- It prevents **SSL-stripping** downgrade attacks by eliminating the **plaintext first request**.
- Browsers **auto-upgrade** `http://` and **refuse** invalid certificates (no click-through).
- Use **long `max-age` + `includeSubDomains`**; add **`preload`** only when confident.
- It's only honored over **HTTPS**, not plain HTTP.
- Spring Security enables HSTS by default; customize via `headers().httpStrictTransportSecurity(...)`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HSTS, which stands for HTTP Strict Transport Security, is a response header that tells the browser: for the next so-many seconds, only ever connect to this domain over HTTPS. Once the browser has seen that header once, it does two things. First, it automatically upgrades any http link to https before it even sends the request. And second, if the certificate is invalid, it refuses to connect entirely — there's no click-through to ignore the warning.

The attack it's designed to stop is called SSL stripping. The problem is that normally a site redirects a plain http request to https, but that very first plaintext request is a window of opportunity. A man-in-the-middle on the network can intercept it, keep the user's connection on plain HTTP while quietly talking HTTPS to the real server, and the user never realizes their traffic isn't encrypted. HSTS closes that window, because once the policy is cached, the browser never makes the plaintext request in the first place — it goes straight to HTTPS.

You configure it with a few directives: max-age, which is how long to enforce it, usually something like a year; includeSubDomains, which extends the policy to all your subdomains; and optionally preload, which gets your domain hardcoded into the browsers' built-in lists so that even a user's very first visit is protected. The important caution I'd mention is that you should only turn on preload and a long max-age once you're confident HTTPS works everywhere, because if HTTPS later breaks, browsers won't fall back to HTTP and you can lock users out. Also, HSTS is only honored over HTTPS — a browser ignores it if you send it over plain HTTP. In Spring Boot, Spring Security actually adds HSTS by default on HTTPS responses, and you can customize the directives through the headers configuration.

beats.label: the ssl stripping attack
beats.content: Users sometimes type http:// or click old bookmarks. Your server redirects to HTTPS — but an attacker on the same network can intercept that initial HTTP request and perform SSL stripping: they hold an HTTP connection to the user and proxy to your HTTPS server themselves. The user sees content but has no encryption.

beats.label: how hsts fixes it
beats.content: Once a browser sees the Strict-Transport-Security header, it remembers: never send HTTP to this domain. It upgrades to HTTPS internally before any packet leaves the machine. The attacker has no unencrypted request to intercept. Spring Security adds this header by default with max-age of one year.

beats.label: gotcha
beats.content: gotcha: HSTS breaks local development if you test over HTTP. Disable it in your development Spring profile using http.headers().httpStrictTransportSecurity().disable(). Also, the first visit to a site is still unprotected — that's what the HSTS preload list solves.

question: What are common HTTPS configuration mistakes in Spring Boot?
title: Common HTTPS Configuration Mistakes in Spring Boot
direct_answer: Common HTTPS mistakes in Spring Boot: **not redirecting HTTP to HTTPS** (leaving an open plaintext door), **trusting forwarded headers without configuring `server.forward-headers-strategy`** behind a proxy (so redirects/`secure` flags break), **disabling certificate validation** for outbound calls, **using self-signed certs in production**, **forgetting HSTS**, and **not marking cookies `Secure`** so they leak over any accidental HTTP. The fixes are mostly configuration: force the channel to HTTPS, set the forward-headers strategy, and harden cookies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know practical Spring Boot HTTPS pitfalls beyond 'enable SSL', especially proxy header handling and cookie flags
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Disabling TLS verification to 'make it work', or not handling X-Forwarded headers behind a load balancer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention forward-headers-strategy for proxies, Secure+SameSite cookies, and never disabling hostname/cert verification on RestTemplate/WebClient

sections.title: HTTPS Pitfalls Are Usually Configuration
sections.content:
When HTTPS goes wrong in a Spring Boot app, it's rarely the cryptography — it's **misconfiguration around the edges**. The classics: leaving **plain HTTP reachable** with no redirect; running **behind a reverse proxy/load balancer** that terminates TLS but not telling Spring to **trust the `X-Forwarded-*` headers**, so the app thinks requests are HTTP and generates broken redirects and non-`Secure` cookies; **disabling certificate validation** on outbound `RestTemplate`/`WebClient` calls to silence errors; shipping **self-signed certificates** to production; **forgetting HSTS**; and **not marking session cookies `Secure`** so they can leak over any accidental HTTP request.

The good news is the fixes are mostly **a few lines of config**: force the channel to HTTPS, set `server.forward-headers-strategy`, harden cookies with `Secure`/`HttpOnly`/`SameSite`, and never turn off TLS verification.

sections.title: HTTPS Misconfig Hot Spots
sections.content:
rose|Open HTTP|~No redirect|plaintext door left open|fix: requiresSecure()|force HTTPS
blue|Proxy headers|~Wrong scheme|TLS ends at load balancer|forward-headers-strategy|app sees real HTTPS
amber|Cookie flags|~Leak risk|missing Secure flag|Secure+HttpOnly+SameSite|never sent over HTTP
emerald|TLS verification|~Never disable|trusting any cert = MITM|fix trust store instead|keep hostname checks

sections.title: The Fix Checklist
sections.content:
| # | Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | HTTP left open | `requiresChannel().anyRequest().requiresSecure()` to force HTTPS |
| 2 | Behind proxy, wrong scheme | `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework` (or `native`) |
| 3 | Cookies leak over HTTP | `server.servlet.session.cookie.secure=true` + `same-site=lax` |
| 4 | No HSTS | enable `httpStrictTransportSecurity` in Spring Security |
| 5 | Self-signed in prod | use a CA-issued cert (e.g. Let's Encrypt) |
| 6 | TLS verification disabled | never disable hostname/cert checks on outbound clients |

sections.title: Anti-pattern: disabling TLS verification
Correct: force HTTPS + trust proxy headers + secure cookies
sections.content:
```java
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http
        .requiresChannel(c -> c.anyRequest().requiresSecure())  // HTTP -> HTTPS
        .headers(h -> h.httpStrictTransportSecurity(hsts -> hsts.maxAgeInSeconds(31536000)));
    return http.build();
}
```
```properties
# Behind a load balancer that terminates TLS: trust the forwarded scheme
server.forward-headers-strategy=framework
# Cookies only over HTTPS, not readable by JS, not sent cross-site
server.servlet.session.cookie.secure=true
server.servlet.session.cookie.http-only=true
server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=lax
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Disabling cert/hostname validation** to make outbound HTTPS calls work — this re-enables MITM.
- **Ignoring `X-Forwarded-*`** behind a proxy — Spring thinks it's HTTP and breaks redirects/cookies.
- **Non-`Secure` cookies** — a single accidental HTTP request leaks the session.
- **Self-signed certs in production** — browsers/clients reject them; use a real CA.
- **No HTTP→HTTPS redirect** — leaves a plaintext entry point even when HTTPS is available.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Redirect HTTP to HTTPS** with `requiresChannel().requiresSecure()`.
- Behind a proxy, set **`server.forward-headers-strategy`** so Spring sees the real HTTPS scheme.
- Mark cookies **`Secure` + `HttpOnly` + `SameSite`** so they never leak over HTTP.
- **Enable HSTS** and use **CA-issued** certificates in production.
- **Never disable TLS certificate/hostname validation** on `RestTemplate`/`WebClient`.
- Most HTTPS bugs are **configuration**, not cryptography.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When HTTPS goes wrong in a Spring Boot app, it's almost never the cryptography itself — it's misconfiguration around the edges. The first common mistake is leaving plain HTTP reachable with no redirect, so even though HTTPS is available, there's still an open plaintext door. The fix is to force the channel to be secure, using requiresChannel requiresSecure in Spring Security, so any HTTP request gets redirected to HTTPS.

The second, and probably the most common in real deployments, is running behind a reverse proxy or load balancer that terminates TLS, but not telling Spring to trust the forwarded headers. The proxy talks HTTPS to the client but plain HTTP to your app, and if you don't set server dot forward-headers-strategy, Spring thinks the original request was HTTP. That breaks generated redirect URLs and means cookies don't get marked Secure. So setting that property correctly is important.

A third one is around cookies — if you don't mark your session cookie as Secure, it can leak over any accidental HTTP request. So I'd set Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite on it. Then there's forgetting HSTS, and shipping self-signed certificates to production instead of a proper CA-issued certificate like Let's Encrypt. But the most dangerous mistake of all is when people disable certificate or hostname validation on outbound calls — for example on a RestTemplate — just to make an HTTPS call work without errors. That completely defeats the purpose of TLS, because it re-opens man-in-the-middle attacks. You should never do that; instead you fix the trust store. So the theme is that the fixes are mostly a few lines of configuration: force HTTPS, handle proxy headers, harden cookies, enable HSTS, and never turn off TLS verification.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with OWASP-compliant security
speakable_v2.hook: Most Spring Boot HTTPS bugs aren't crypto — they're a missing redirect, an unconfigured proxy header, or a cookie that forgot to be Secure.

beats.label: common pitfalls
beats.content:
The mistakes I see most often:
- TLS termination done in Spring Boot directly instead of at the load balancer or Nginx
- Spring Boot not configured to trust X-Forwarded-Proto, so it thinks every request is HTTP even though Nginx is handling HTTPS
- HTTP port 8080 left open alongside 443 — attacker just uses 8080
- No HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect configured
- Certificate expiry not automated — Certbot handles renewal for Let's Encrypt certs

beats.label: x-forwarded-proto
beats.content: The X-Forwarded-Proto issue catches many developers off guard. When Nginx handles TLS, Spring Boot only sees the internal HTTP request. Your redirect logic and HSTS headers break because Spring thinks the connection is already HTTP. Fix it with server.forward-headers-strategy=native in application.properties.

beats.label: production trap
beats.content: production trap: self-signed certs in production. They work technically but browsers show security warnings and some HTTP clients reject them outright. Use Let's Encrypt. Run SSL Labs on your domain before launch — it checks protocol versions, cipher suites, certificate chain, and HSTS in one scan.
